comments.author: _fw
comments.text: I appreciate their reluctance towards MCP, but /something/ is better than nothing. It’s suboptimal for the reasons the author outlines: but so is USB-C. So is NVME, so is HDMI. We use these hugely successful technologies in spite of their flaws because they’re widely compatible and easy for the end user. That’s why MCP is everywhere. It might not be performant, robust and uniform but it WILL get better over time. And I’d much rather have the broad MCP ecosystem that we have now than seven or eight different “optimal” ways of plugging in an LLM to something useful.

comments.author: wren6991
comments.text: > And while we could have just wired up the metadata to enable better MCP extensions, we also think that MCP with Codemode solves quite a few of the issues that it traditionally had. There's just something that bothers me about this. Normally if LLMs want to compose multiple operations, they have the perfect tool for this: bash, or whatever other OS shell is available. It's why I was always confused by Codemode-type constructs for direct chaining of tool calls; see also the way highly-RL'd modern models will fall back to sed or python for complex file edits. It seems like Codemode is raised here as the perfect tool for chaining or composing MCPs, but isn't that backwards? LLMs are already given the perfect tool for that, and the problem is that MCPs aren't exposed to that tool.

49905487.title: September 2026: The world today, as seen by one Polish guy

comments.author: roenxi
comments.text: > Every generation believes it is living through the end of something. Many generations are. Last century saw the collapse of the British and Soviet empires - titans by any measure - through mismanagement. Europe as an international power was also broken (compared to how they used to be). I can easily imagine 1900s me fleeing to America in fear of the end times and feeling quite justified in his choices with hindsight. Less obvious where to run to these days as the US not-an-empire looks like it may crumble. Most of the people who died didn't get an opportunity to complain, so we live with some serious survivorship bias on how bad things got.

comments.author: harrouet
comments.text: This how empires collapse: - To maintain fellowship, the empire spreads money to buy influence - eventually this starts to cost too much, so the empire reduces spending - wars ensue and independent voices emerge - unable to establish order, the empire loses its influence and collapses You can see this patterns as the US is overspending (high debt / trade deficit) while reducing its diplomatic influence on international programs. Not sure how they can save the USD value over time.

comments.author: PersonalJarvis

comments.author: lifestyleguru
comments.text: Criminals and medical doctors are funnelling a fortune into domestic and foreign real estate, and into premium cars. Polish public healthcare basically doesn't exist. Nearshoring and outsourcing centers are fleeing the country. Polish army expenditures are at the level of Israel and South Korea. The budget is spent on 40 years old military retirees while Russian drones and missiles are freely entering and penetrating the airspace. I'd say so long Poland, a failed experiment again. Polish elites don't even have to flee this time, they're already watching from their 10th or 20th real estate in Spain, Switzerland, US, or Italy (their real estate in Dubai is a bummer). This technical analysis is really futile and counterproductive, there exists only vicious greed which will be followed by a catastrophe.

49907057.title: Most data centers refusing to say how much water, electricity they use

comments.author: stingraycharles
comments.text: Playing the devil’s advocate: don’t “freedom of information” laws mostly apply to government agencies? If so, why would a private company provide this information? I personally believe at the very least the water usage is heavily overblown compared to the agriculture industry. Elecricity is a different issue, and governments should consider reporting requirements or something like that. Being angry with datacenter providers is not the solution. And they also need to be built somewhere , and that place is probably best where electricity is abundant and/or cheap.

comments.author: petcat
comments.text: EU is in such a weird position. They are realizing that software, robotics, and generally automation through AI is the industrial future, but they seem to be paralyzed to actually start the build-up that will feed that frontier industry and economy.

comments.author: unglaublich
comments.text: They refuse it because if they would say "1 million liters a year!" the knee-jerk reaction will be completely predictable even though that's just tiny compared to a small swimming pool or industrial or agricultural site. The debate is completely based on emotion and anger right now, so sharing information will only give the emotional/angry folks more mud to throw with. The majority of people has no clue about how to put things like energy use and water use in perspective, and they're also not interested in doing that. Because they have decided to green-wash their AI-fears as environmental fears... which is a big fat joke because datacenters aren't significant polluters or consumers compared to almost all other industries. Look, I get it, many people are afraid of the societal impacts of AI, or distrust it in another way. But let's be honest and focus on _that_ instead of naively acting as if our anti-datacenter sentiment comes from environmental concerns (the last few decades have shown we don't GAF about the environment).

comments.author: zug_zug
comments.text: And my great great grandpa thought horses would lose all their jobs to cars. And they all did and it was never the same again. There’s no quick answers, but intuitively I think we all get that the % of jobs not doable by AI and robotics approaches 0 over time.

comments.author: khalic
comments.text: What a refreshingly positive read

comments.author: glimshe
comments.text: There are two key elements in the current AI fearmongering: 1) People think they can predict the future 2) People think humans can't adapt The number of disruptive "game changing" technologies throughout history is immense. There's no question some people get negatively affected, but humanity as a whole has prospered because of these disruptions. Literally every time, including during the industrial revolution, people thought it was game over for society, good manners, the youth, the planet etc. Keep cool and try to adapt to the inevitable change. The next generation will certainly do it and leave you behind if you stay in a corner denying the new reality.

comments.author: hangrybear666
comments.text: > Many of us, deep down, are driven more by the joy of making things, solving problems, and seeing people use what we built than by the act of coding itself. I've definitely always enjoyed the end-result but only for the fact that it proved I have overcome challenges and slowly but steadily inched one step closer towards mastery. Both are now gone, since mastery is not required and challenges are absent except the soul draining exhaustion of reading markdown all day. Now I'm just producing outcomes for my boss, rather than my own fulfillment. The journey has become a farce, I will ride this out and make my money but I don't care about it much anymore. That being said in my free time, as in Hobby I am doing pentesting manually for fun. Because productivity is irrelevant for my hobbies, so I can still keep inching towards mastery and overcome challenges, at least on days where my job leaves any trace of surplus energy at the end of the day.

comments.author: vintagedave
comments.text: Wow. This is big news for C++. For background -- and I am not an expert here -- their C++ frontend is widely known. I first heard of it because Visual C++'s Intellisense uses it, which was notable because VC does not use the msvc frontend for its own completion. I understand it's been either used or evaluated for other frontends in the past too. I worked as PM for one C++ product, and was fortunate to be able to learn a lot from our engineers; we didn't use it, but they thought highly of EDG. It has a very strong reputation for being correct. And as such, I think open sourcing it will be a very beneficial thing for the C++ community.
